title: Before the Startup: six counterintuitive rules Paul Graham would tell his own kids
summary: Graham argues startups are counterintuitive, like skiing, so instincts mislead. Success comes from making something users want, not gaming the system or learning startup mechanics. Don't start one in college; instead learn powerful things and let ideas emerge unconsciously from side projects.

principles.text: What you need is expertise in your own users, not expertise in startups.
principles.quote: What you need to know to suceed in a startup is not expertise in startups, what you need is expertise in your own users.

principles.text: Growth hacks are bullshit; growth comes from making something users love and telling them.
principles.quote: the way to make your startup grow is to make something that users really love. Right, and then tell them about it. So that's what you have to do. That is growth hacks right there.

principles.text: Don't play house: going through the motions of a startup neglects making something people want.
principles.quote: while imitating all the outward forms of starting a startup, they have neglected the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want.

principles.text: Gaming the system stops working in startups because users are too blunt to fool.
principles.quote: There's only users. And all users care about is whether your software. Does what they want, right? They're like sharks.

principles.text: Best way to convince investors is to grow fast; tricks matter an order of magnitude less.
principles.quote: the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning growing fast, and then simply tell investors so.

principles.text: Don't try to think of startup ideas; become the kind of person who has them unconsciously by learning things that matter.
principles.quote: 1, learn about things that matter. 2, work on problems that interest you. 3, with people you like and respect.
